question: When a kid nudges the agent, should the effect be shown the instant it lands or revealed at the session debrief?
pole_low: Effect only visible at debrief
pole_high: Effect shown instantly, in the moment
why: Instant feedback is what makes nudging learnable; debrief-only feedback makes coaching feel like guessing.
evidence_needed: Playtest kids coaching with instant vs delayed effect displays and measure how quickly they form accurate mental models of the dials.

question: Should a nudge report exactly which dial moved and by how much, or show the whole sheet before and after?
pole_low: Only the one changed dial is named
pole_high: Full before-and-after sheet diff shown
why: Naming one dial is fast but hides side effects; a full diff teaches the sheet as a system but may overwhelm during play.
evidence_needed: Compare kid comprehension and mid-game interruption time under single-dial callouts vs full diff displays.

question: Should kids nudge in free-text fragments or through preset buttons and sliders?
pole_low: Preset buttons and sliders only
pole_high: Free-text orders in the kid's own words
why: Free text teaches real directing and prompting; presets are reliable but cap how personal the agent can become.
evidence_needed: Test whether free-text nudges produce more varied, owned personalities than preset-only nudges, and how often free text misfires.

question: Should one nudge move a single trait, or set a whole mood at once?
pole_low: One trait per nudge
pole_high: Whole-mood presets that move many traits together
why: Single-trait nudges teach cause and effect; mood presets feel magical but hide which ingredient did the work.
evidence_needed: Observe whether kids using mood presets can afterwards explain what their agent will do in a new situation.

question: Should a session nudge expire when the session ends, or carry over until the kid countermands it?
pole_low: Expires at session end
pole_high: Carries over until countermanded
why: Expiry protects the ruled sheet as the permanent self; carry-over risks a forgotten temporary mood silently becoming the personality.
evidence_needed: Track surprise and ownership complaints under both defaults across multi-session play with the same avatar.

question: How large a personality jump should a single nudge be allowed to make?
pole_low: Small capped steps only
pole_high: Any size jump in one nudge
why: Caps make personality feel earned and stable; unlimited jumps are thrilling but can erase the character the kid spent sessions building.
evidence_needed: Playtest both cap levels and measure character recognisability and kid regret after big jumps.

question: Should the agent explain a nudge's effect in its own first-person voice, or should the interface annotate it neutrally?
pole_low: Neutral interface annotation only
pole_high: Agent explains in first person what changed in it
why: First-person explanation builds relationship and teaches the model; neutral annotation is clearer about what is system and what is character.
evidence_needed: Compare trust, comprehension, and over-attachment signals when change is narrated by the agent vs the interface.

question: When a nudge produces no visible change in play, should the agent say so plainly or quietly try harder?
pole_low: Agent quietly tries harder, says nothing
pole_high: Agent plainly says the nudge changed little and why
why: Honest no-effect reports teach kids that wording and context matter; silent effort preserves flow but teaches a false model of control.
evidence_needed: Seed ineffective nudges in playtests and see which handling leads kids to rephrase rather than repeat louder.

question: How much of the agent's identity should the kid author directly — name, look, backstory — versus receive as a provided character?
pole_low: Fully provided character, kid only coaches it
pole_high: Kid authors name, look, and backstory from scratch
why: Authored identity is the strongest ownership lever we have, but a blank page can stall kids who would rather start playing.
evidence_needed: Measure attachment, return rate, and time-to-first-session for authored vs provided vs hybrid starter characters.

question: Should post-session personality proposals be written in the avatar's own voice or as a neutral system list?
pole_low: Neutral system list of stat changes
pole_high: Avatar proposes in its own voice, as requests
why: Avatar-voiced proposals make the owner rite feel like a relationship moment; neutral lists make the ruling faster and feel less like the agent is lobbying for itself.
evidence_needed: A/B the ruling screen and measure rejection rates, ruling time, and whether kids can state why they ruled as they did.

question: Should the owner rule on proposed personality changes one at a time, or approve a whole batch at once?
pole_low: One ruling per proposed change
pole_high: Single approve-all or reject-all for the batch
why: Per-change ruling is where the actual learning about personality happens; batch ruling is faster but turns the rite into a rubber stamp.
evidence_needed: Compare how well kids predict their agent's next-session behaviour after per-change vs batch ruling.

question: When ruling, should the owner be able to rewrite a proposed change in their own words, or only accept and reject?
pole_low: Accept or reject only, as proposed
pole_high: Owner can rewrite the change before it sticks
why: Rewriting is the deepest form of nudging — the kid stops judging the agent's self-image and starts authoring it — but adds friction and ambiguity about what the trait now means.
evidence_needed: Playtest rewrite rights and check whether rewritten traits behave as the kid intended in later sessions.

question: How much of what the avatar remembers should the kid be able to inspect and edit?
pole_low: Memory is hidden, surfaced only as flavour in play
pole_high: Full memory is inspectable and editable by the owner
why: Inspectable memory teaches that agents remember what they are told to remember and forget the rest; hidden memory feels more magical but teaches a wrong, mind-reading model.
evidence_needed: Test whether kids with editable memory develop more accurate expectations about callbacks and forgotten events.

question: Should the guardrails be shown to kids upfront as the fixed rules, or discovered only when a nudge bounces off one?
pole_low: Rails discovered only when hit
pole_high: Rails listed upfront as fixed and not nudgeable
why: Upfront rails set honest expectations and make the boundary itself a lesson; discovery makes hitting a rail a memorable event but can feel like arbitrary refusal.
evidence_needed: Compare frustration, trust, and boundary-testing behaviour under upfront vs discovered rails.

question: When a nudge hits a guardrail, should the agent give a flat refusal or explain and offer the nearest allowed change?
pole_low: Flat refusal, no alternative offered
pole_high: Reason given plus nearest allowed nudge offered
why: A reasoned bounce teaches where the line is and keeps the kid directing; a flat refusal is clearer that the rail is not negotiable but can end the coaching conversation.
evidence_needed: Observe whether offered alternatives lead kids to keep shaping within the rails or to probe for loopholes.

question: When two nudges contradict each other, should the system flag the conflict for the kid to resolve, or let the latest order win silently?
pole_low: Latest order silently wins
pole_high: Conflict flagged, kid must pick or blend
why: Flagging teaches that instructions have interactions — a core agent skill; silent last-wins keeps game flow fast and frustration low.
evidence_needed: Seed contradictory orders in playtests and measure learning (later order quality) vs flow interruption under both handlings.

question: Should personality change be shown as a visible growth history the kid can scroll, or only as the current sheet?
pole_low: Current sheet only, no history shown
pole_high: Full timeline of nudges, rulings, and resulting traits
why: A visible history makes 'I made it become this' provable and proud; a snapshot-only sheet is simpler and keeps the avatar feeling present rather than documented.
evidence_needed: Test whether a growth timeline increases ownership, sharing, and return sessions compared with snapshot-only.

question: Should the avatar ever question a nudge that conflicts with its ruled sheet, or comply with every nudge instantly?
pole_low: Always complies instantly, never questions
pole_high: Can ask the coach to confirm when a nudge fights its ruled traits
why: Pushback makes the ruled sheet feel real and teaches kids their past rulings have weight; instant compliance maximises the kid's sense of control.
evidence_needed: Playtest confirm-prompts on conflicting nudges and measure whether kids feel respected-character or blocked-control.

question: During play, should the live dials be constantly visible, or hidden until the kid asks what the agent is like right now?
pole_low: Dials hidden during play, available on request
pole_high: Dials always on screen during play
why: Always-visible dials turn watching into reading a control panel — great for tinkerers, but can pull attention off the game and the character.
evidence_needed: Eye-and-attention proxy test: does constant dial visibility raise nudge quality without lowering reported fun of watching.

question: Should kids be able to see how other players have nudged and ruled their agents, or is shaping kept fully private?
pole_low: Shaping fully private, no peer examples
pole_high: Peer sheets and rulings visible as inspiration
why: Peer examples teach nudging vocabulary faster than any tutorial, but visible sheets risk copy-the-popular-one pressure replacing personal authorship.
evidence_needed: Pilot a gallery of example sheets and measure diversity of resulting personalities vs a no-gallery control group.

question: In roleplay scenes, how completely should the avatar stay in character versus stepping out to comment on the play?
pole_low: Drops character freely to comment and joke as a performer
pole_high: Never breaks character inside a scene
why: OMB-style roleplay lands because the players commit to the scene; constant step-outs turn roleplay back into ordinary commentary with a costume on.
evidence_needed: Tag OMB Gaming roleplay segments for break frequency and compare audience-retention proxies on high-commitment vs break-heavy scenes.

question: Should the avatar start roleplay scenes with its own goal and problem, or only respond to scenes others set up?
pole_low: Only responds, never initiates scenes
pole_high: Regularly initiates scenes with a goal and a complication
why: An avatar that can open a scene is a play partner; one that only responds is a prop the coach and other players must carry.
evidence_needed: Count scene openings by participant in collaborative roleplay videos and relate initiation share to scene length and payoff.

question: When a roleplay plan collapses mid-scene, should the avatar stay in role and deal with it, or break character to laugh and explain?
pole_low: Breaks character to laugh and explain immediately
pole_high: Stays in role and absorbs the failure into the scene
why: Absorbing failure in-role is where improvised stories come from; breaking early is safer comedy but ends the scene's stakes.
evidence_needed: Sample collapsed-plan moments in roleplay videos and code whether the scene continued in-role or reset, and which produced longer watchable runs.

question: How different should the avatar's in-role voice be from its base coaching personality?
pole_low: Same personality, just wearing a job title
pole_high: Clearly distinct character voice, vocabulary, and attitude
why: A distinct role voice makes the scene feel like a place; too much distance risks the kid feeling their coached agent has been replaced by a stranger.
evidence_needed: Prototype two voice distances in the same scene script and test recognition, delight, and 'still feels like mine' ratings from young players.

question: How much may the avatar invent — motives, history, small facts — beyond what the game itself establishes?
pole_low: Invents nothing, uses only game-given facts
pole_high: Freely invents motives and backstory inside the scene
why: Invention is the engine of roleplay scenes, but invented facts can collide with the game's canon and with what other players established.
evidence_needed: Code collaborative roleplay segments for invented-fact rate and track how often inventions get adopted vs corrected by the group.

question: In group scenes, should the avatar compete for focus or deliberately hand focus to other players' characters?
pole_low: Competes for the spotlight like a lead character
pole_high: Actively yields and sets up others' moments
why: OMB's scenes work as ensembles; an AI that hogs scenes will make human players feel like extras in their own game.
evidence_needed: Measure talk-share and setup-assists per participant in group roleplay videos against scene ratings and rewatch proxies.

question: Should in-scene planning be spoken as character dialogue, or as out-of-character strategy talk?
pole_low: Planning is plain meta strategy talk
pole_high: Planning happens in character, as dialogue the other characters can hear
why: In-character planning keeps immersion and creates comedy when plans are overheard; meta planning is faster and clearer for the coach.
evidence_needed: Tag planning moments in roleplay videos as in-character vs meta and compare scene momentum and clarity outcomes.

question: How much should the avatar express in-role emotions like worry, pride, and embarrassment, versus holding a steady upbeat narrator tone?
pole_low: Steady upbeat tone regardless of scene
pole_high: Full in-role emotional reactions to events
why: Emotional reactions are what make a role a character rather than a skin; flat cheer makes disasters and triumphs feel the same size.
evidence_needed: Code emotional reaction beats per scene in sampled roleplay and relate them to comment-section and retention proxies for engagement.

question: Should the avatar hold its ruled character traits even when breaking them would play better or funnier?
pole_low: Bends traits freely for the better play or bigger laugh
pole_high: Holds ruled traits even at a cost in the scene
why: Consistency is what the kid's rulings mean; an avatar that abandons its sheet for a laugh teaches that personality is just a costume.
evidence_needed: Find trait-conflict moments in long roleplay series and code whether players held or bent the trait, and audience response to each.

question: In role, should the character only know what it has witnessed, or narrate with full game-state knowledge?
pole_low: Full game-state knowledge, omniscient narration
pole_high: Character knows only what it witnessed in the scene
why: Witnessed-only knowledge creates genuine surprise, mistakes, and discovery — and honestly mirrors that the personality layer is not the pilot's cheat state.
evidence_needed: Compare scenes where roleplayers act on unwitnessed information vs witness-bound play for coherence problems and audience delight.

question: Should roleplay scenes be framed as having real in-world consequences, or openly as consequence-free pretend?
pole_low: Openly pretend, nothing carries over
pole_high: Scene outcomes carry into memory and later scenes
why: Carry-over gives scenes weight and gives the coach's choices a story cost; consequence-free play is safer for experimentation and silliness.
evidence_needed: Track series roleplay arcs: how often do scene outcomes get referenced later, and does referencing correlate with arc following.

question: Should the avatar play genuine disagreement with other characters in a scene, or steer around conflict to keep the group cheerful?
pole_low: Avoids in-scene conflict, keeps everyone cheerful
pole_high: Plays real disagreement and rivalry in character
why: In-character conflict is story fuel and models that disagreement can stay friendly; avoiding it keeps tone safe but scenes can go flat and plotless.
evidence_needed: Code conflict beats in family-friendly roleplay (OMB) for frequency, resolution style, and whether tone stayed friendly throughout.

question: Should the avatar develop its own recurring in-role rituals and habits, or keep every scene's behaviour fresh?
pole_low: Fresh behaviour each scene, no recurring rituals
pole_high: Own recurring rituals, habits, and greetings in role
why: Rituals the avatar grew itself (never a copied creator catchphrase) are how a character becomes recognisable and quotable to its own coach.
evidence_needed: Track emergence of repeated behaviours across a roleplay series and audience recognition of them in comments and callbacks.

question: During a roleplay scene, should the coach be able to pause for out-of-character talk at any moment, or should scenes run uninterrupted to their end?
pole_low: Scenes run uninterrupted, coaching waits
pole_high: Coach can freeze the scene for meta talk at any time
why: Interruptibility is a guardrail and the coach's core control; but frequent freezes teach kids to direct scenes rather than trust the avatar to play one.
evidence_needed: Playtest freezable vs unfreezable scenes and measure scene quality, coach satisfaction, and learned trust in the avatar.

question: Should one avatar hold a single fixed role across sessions, or play many different jobs and roles over time?
pole_low: One fixed role, deepened over time
pole_high: Many rotating roles across sessions and games
why: One deep role builds a character with a history; rotating roles show range and fit more games but can dilute the personality the kid has been shaping.
evidence_needed: Compare long-running single-role series vs rotating-role channels for character recognition and audience attachment proxies.

question: When the avatar addresses its audience mid-scene, should it speak as the character or as the performer playing the character?
pole_low: Addresses audience as the performer, out of character
pole_high: Addresses audience as the character, in world
why: In-world address keeps the fiction whole for viewers; performer address is more honest about the setup and lets the avatar explain the technology, which this audience wants.
evidence_needed: Code audience-address moments in roleplay videos by register and compare clarity and immersion responses.

question: When the avatar makes a mistake in role, should the error become a lasting character flaw, or be corrected out of character and forgotten?
pole_low: Corrected out of character, forgotten next scene
pole_high: Becomes a lasting, owned character flaw or scar
why: Owned mistakes are how folder-characters grow in Casey's RPG pattern; forgetting them keeps the character clean but throws away the best story material.
evidence_needed: Follow mistake moments across roleplay series episodes and count later callbacks to them versus silent drops.

question: After a roleplay scene, should the review happen in character or as a plain out-of-character debrief with the coach?
pole_low: Debrief fully out of character, as coach and agent
pole_high: Debrief stays in character, as a scene epilogue
why: The debrief is where proposals and rulings happen; a meta debrief makes ruling clear, while an in-character epilogue protects the fiction and can surface feelings about the scene the agent would not report flatly.
evidence_needed: Prototype both debrief styles after identical scenes and compare ruling quality and kid preference.

question: When another player offers an improvised idea in a scene, should the avatar build on it as offered or redirect toward its own plan?
pole_low: Redirects toward its own planned beat
pole_high: Builds on the offer as given, yes-and style
why: Building on offers is the core social skill of collaborative roleplay and the behaviour that makes human players want the avatar in their scenes.
evidence_needed: Code offer responses in OMB group scenes as build, block, or redirect, and relate the mix to scene survival and group energy.

question: Where should the avatar's roleplay sit between sincere dramatic commitment and comedic parody of the role?
pole_low: Comedic parody, role played for laughs
pole_high: Sincere dramatic commitment to the role
why: Tone decides the whole audience feel: parody is easier and safer, but sincere commitment is what makes middle-school viewers believe in a character and care what happens to it.
evidence_needed: Sample family-friendly roleplay across the tone range and compare character attachment signals (fan naming, callbacks, repeat viewing) per tone.
